newsitem.title: UK: GROBBELAAR SAID FILMED TAKING CASH TO FIX GAMES.
newsitem.headline: GROBBELAAR SAID FILMED TAKING CASH TO FIX GAMES.

text.p: Secret film of former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar taking 2,000 pounds ($3,300) from what the prosecution says was a bogus betting syndicate he thought wanted him to rig soccer matches was shown in court on Tuesday.

Jurors watched videotapes of conversations between Grobbelaar and prosecution witness Chris Vincent, who was pretending to be the front man for the syndicate. The tapes were covertly recorded by the Sun tabloid newspaper.
In one film, Grobbelaar could be seen picking up a packet alleged to contain the money and putting it in his pocket.

The prosecution says Grobbelaar, one of four men on trial for match-fixing in the most sensational case of its kind in Britain for 30 years, tried to rig four games for an Asian betting syndicate while playing for Liverpool and Southampton.
Grobbelaar and the other accused have all pleaded not guilty to the match-rigging charges.
Vincent says he was with Grobbelaar when he received 40,000 pounds in late 1993 for throwing an away match against Newcastle when still playing for Liverpool.
Vincent told Grobbelaar the mythical syndicate would pay him 2,000 pounds every two weeks to predict the results of games, plus a further 100,000 pounds for rigging each match.
Another tape records him deciding to accept Vincent's offer, according to the prosecution.

"Right, I've heard enough. I've had enough now. We'll make this easy. Tell him that's on, and I'm going to pick one game. I'll pick one game...after I've picked the game nothing must be said," he could be heard saying."
Other comments indicate the goalkeeper had deep reservations about the scheme, according to the prosecution.
"This is dangerous, it is. I'm telling you, this is how dangerous it is. When you're playing with dangerous men, it's dangerous," he said, littering his speech with expletives.

Vincent said Grobbelaar told him that co-defendant and former Wimbledon striker John Fashanu -- accused of being a middleman for the syndicate -- had made a surprise move to Aston Villa in 1994 because match-fixing had become too risky.

Vincent, a former business partner of Grobbelaar until the two men fell out in 1994, said the keeper had also told him he had been promised money for losing a game which Southampton played against Manchester City in early November 1994.

He said he had been present when Grobbelaar took a phone call from a syndicate middleman he dubbed the "Short Man". The prosecution say the "Short Man" is Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim, who is also on trial.

"Grobbelaar said: 'That was the Short Man and this weekend we are going to lose by one'. He said they were starting small again and he was only going to get 25,000 pounds," Vincent told the court in the south-western city of Winchester.
In a tape recorded just before the game at Manchester City, Grobbelaar can be heard saying the Short Man was now prepared to pay 50,000 pounds. The game ended in a 3-3 draw.
The other man on trial is former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers, accused with Lim and Fashanu of taking part in a separate bid to fix matches. All four pleaded not guilty.
